events.title: Detecting and Patching Log4j (Log4Shell): A Practical Playbook
events.summary: A community-published playbook explains how defenders can detect and patch Log4j (Log4Shell), using the vulnerability as a template for understanding how a logging library can become a remote code execution vector. It recounts the mechanism: a logged attacker-controlled string could trigger a JNDI lookup and make the application connect to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
events.why_it_matters: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) is rated critical with a CVSS of 10.0, is listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerability catalogue, and has an EPSS score near the maximum, indicating extremely high exploitation likelihood. The record notes it remains a reference point for intrusion analysis more than four years after disclosure. Defenders can use the playbook as a model for building detection guidance against similar library-level RCE flaws.

claims.text: CISA lists CVE-2021-44228 as exploited in the wild, added 2021-12-10, with US federal agencies due to fix it by 2021-12-24.
CVE-2021-44228 is rated 10.0 (critical) under CVSS 3.1 by CISA in the CVE record.
FIRST's EPSS puts the chance of CVE-2021-44228 being exploited in the next 30 days at 100%.
A fix for org.apache.logging.log4j:log4j-core (Maven) is published in 2.15.0, 2.3.1 and 2.12.2, per GHSA-jfh8-c2jp-5v3q.
A fix for org.ops4j.pax.logging:pax-logging-log4j2 (Maven) is published in 1.9.2, 1.10.8, 1.11.10 and 2.0.11, per GHSA-jfh8-c2jp-5v3q.
No fixed version of com.guicedee.services:log4j-core (Maven) is published yet, per GHSA-jfh8-c2jp-5v3q.

Organisations running Keycloak should watch for vendor guidance and confirm whether their SAML configuration is affected.

events.why_it_matters: The incident shows AI-assisted tooling being used at scale against financial institutions' internet-facing systems, with a large volume of personal and financial data exposed. It highlights the value of infrastructure tracing (as Hunt.io did) and the need to harden externally reachable services.

events.title: GhostMap: The Android Crash-Loop Bug With No Patch Yet
events.summary: Bitdefender researchers have disclosed an unpatched Android bug, dubbed GhostMap, that can trap a phone in a crash loop once a single specially crafted app is installed — and that app needs no special permissions. With no fix available, affected devices could be rendered unusable until a patch lands.
events.why_it_matters: The flaw requires no permissions, so users cannot rely on permission prompts as a warning sign when installing apps. With no patch released and a vendor disclosure already public, attackers have a window to weaponise it against Android devices. Defenders may want to flag this to mobile users while awaiting a vendor fix.

events.title: Stealing more than the spotlight.
events.summary: Threat actors are using excitement around the upcoming release of Grand Theft Auto VI to spread malware disguised as leaked game downloads. Huntress researchers found malicious ISO files promoted via search engine poisoning, gaming forums, torrent sites and social media, containing RATs, an infostealer and ransomware that can steal credentials.
events.why_it_matters: Malware delivered through these downloads combines multiple threats — RATs, infostealers and ransomware — meaning a single infection can lead to credential theft and broader compromise. Defenders should be aware that attackers ride hype cycles and poison search results, so users seeking popular content may bypass normal caution. Organisations with gaming staff on work devices could see this malware introduced into their environments.

events.why_it_matters: Front-end weaknesses such as missing CSP and clickjacking protection can let attackers inject scripts or trick users into approving malicious token transfers, as shown by the roughly $120M BadgerDAO loss and the Ledger Connect Kit wallet-drainer incident. Defenders and DeFi users should treat the website itself, not just audited contracts, as part of the attack surface. No specific vulnerabilities, CVEs or active attacks were observed in this passive scan.

events.title: My On-Call Agent Remembered the Rollback That Never Works
events.summary: An engineer describes an on-call LLM agent that gave a better incident-response answer on a second try because it could recall past incidents, including evidence that rollbacks for that service had previously failed. The difference was memory, not the model, which motivated the author's incident-memory agent Déjà Vu.
events.why_it_matters: This is a practitioner account of agent memory improving operational decisions: the memory-equipped agent avoided repeating a rollback that prior incidents (INC-2291, INC-2347) showed was ineffective. For teams deploying AI agents in incident response, it suggests past-incident context can materially change recommendations. The record gives no security findings or deployment details beyond the author's description.

events.title: Why Human Documentation Fails Coding Agents (And How I Asked Gemini, Claude, and OpenAI to Fix It)
events.summary: A developer writes about their experience using LLM coding agents on large, mature Rust codebases, where the tools tend to introduce subtle bugs, stylistic changes, and unsafe simplifications, and describes asking several major models for help with the problem.
events.why_it_matters: The record is a practitioner's account that LLM coding agents perform well on small new projects but degrade on complex existing codebases, producing subtle bugs and dangerous simplifications. This is a caution for teams adopting AI coding assistants in mature codebases with strict security boundaries. No vendor response, benchmark, or safety finding beyond the author's anecdote is given.

events.title: Use browser descriptions to choose, then verify the live account
events.summary: A browser-automation team proposes an operating procedure for AI agents working in web accounts: use recorded browser descriptions to pick the right destination, then separately verify the currently active account before acting. The examples are fictional and no real portal test is claimed.

events.title: Types of Vulnerability Scanning: External, Internal & Credentialed
events.summary: A security blog post from Ciphers Security explains different approaches to vulnerability scanning, covering external versus internal scans, credentialed versus non-credentialed, active versus passive, and agent-based, cloud and container scanning.

events.title: MetaMask addresses infrastructure security incident
events.summary: MetaMask has confirmed a security incident in its infrastructure that led to staking rewards being diverted away from their intended recipients. The record gives no detail on the scope, method, or affected users.
events.why_it_matters: A crypto wallet provider confirming an infrastructure compromise is notable for anyone relying on third-party staking services, since even rewards flows can be tampered with. The record does not state how many users were affected or whether funds beyond staking rewards were touched.

events.title: Six Chartbrew CVEs, One Playbook: Patch, Rotate, Check
events.summary: A security community post walks through six newly published Chartbrew advisories, whose CVE records became active in early November 2026, and recommends a fix order for the vulnerabilities. The flaws range from a default signing secret to an attack path allowing brute forcing of public dashboards.
events.why_it_matters: Organisations running Chartbrew are urged to patch, rotate any exposed secrets, and check their instances, with the flaws covering both authentication material and brute-forceable dashboard access. No CVSS score or evidence of exploitation in the wild appears in the record, so urgency rests on the number of issues disclosed at once.

events.title: Securing Multi-Tenant Kubernetes on AWS: mTLS, Network Policies, and Real Isolation
events.summary: A community article discusses the challenges of securing multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters on AWS, arguing that shared nodes, control planes and network overlays mean the network boundary is effectively already breached. It recommends protocol-level mutual trust between services, mutual TLS and network policies to stop one compromised tenant workload from affecting others.
events.why_it_matters: The piece frames lateral movement between tenants in shared clusters as the core threat rather than perimeter intrusion, noting most clusters lack service-level trust controls. Defenders running shared Kubernetes environments can use its guidance on network policies and mTLS to limit blast radius if one workload is compromised. It reflects general practice guidance rather than a specific incident or vulnerability.

events.title: 499 requests called themselves AI bots on our site in 14 days. We could verify 105.
events.summary: A website operator measured AI crawler traffic to its own site over two weeks and found that only about a fifth of requests claiming to be well-known AI bots could be verified against the operators' published IP lists, with the rest coming from unlisted addresses or being unverifiable. The finding suggests many requests impersonating AI crawlers do not match official identification methods.
events.why_it_matters: Site operators who gate access or content licensing on bot verification may be making decisions based on unverifiable or spoofed crawler identities, with 218 of 499 requests impossible to check at all. This highlights gaps in published IP-based verification as a trust mechanism for AI agents.

reasons: Measured on a non-Australian site with no Australian detail
Global issue with no Australian connection shown

events.title: Building SolShield AI: Byte-Level Honeypot & Rug Defense for Solana AI Agents
events.summary: A community post describes a tool called SolShield AI, aimed at protecting autonomous AI trading agents on Solana from rug-pull and honeypot tokens by analysing tokens at the byte level before transactions are signed. It is a technical write-up of a defensive engineering approach rather than a report of an incident or vulnerability.
events.why_it_matters: The post highlights a claimed risk that AI trading agents cannot distinguish malicious tokens from legitimate ones before signing transactions, meaning automated capital could be lost to rug pulls. Builders of autonomous DeFi agents may see this as an argument for adding pre-transaction token screening. The record provides no evidence of exploited incidents, affected parties, or measured impact.

events.title: The Difference Between a Verification Step and a Reminder to Do One
events.summary: A community blog post reflects on a trending claim that a simple deterministic check can catch issues an AI code reviewer overlooks, because automated code cannot be persuaded to skip the check. The author applies that lesson to their own publishing workflow and finds a verification step they wrote but do not actually enforce.
events.why_it_matters: The piece highlights a practical assurance gap: instructions that ask an AI agent to verify something are not the same as a mechanism that enforces it. For teams using AI agents in workflows, it is a prompt to audit where claimed checks are actually performed. It rests on anecdote, not a documented incident.
